title: Then the friends talk
hookLine: they explain his suffering as punishment, and God later says they were wrong (Job 4–25; 42:7)

lines: IF WE SAY SOMETHING, WILL IT HURT?
A QUESTION THAT LANDS LIKE A VERDICT.
cards: Job speaks first, and what he says is raw. He curses the day he was born. And his friend Eliphaz can't hold it in any longer.
He starts politely, almost shyly: "If we assay to commune with thee, wilt thou be grieved?" In plain words: if we say something, will it upset you? Then he says it anyway.
What follows runs on for chapter after chapter, and it begins with a question that sounds like comfort and lands like a verdict.

teach.b: First, the friends' theory. Eliphaz asks: "Remember, I pray thee, who ever perished, being innocent? or where were the righteous cut off?" Follow that through.
If innocent people don't perish, and Job is perishing, then Job must not be innocent. Bildad and Zophar take their turns, and Eliphaz comes back for more.
The details change, but the shape holds: God is just, so suffering points to wrongdoing; turn back, and things will be restored. Second, Job's answer. He doesn't thank them.

"I have heard many such things: miserable comforters are ye all." And he asks for what they've forgotten how to give: "O that ye would altogether hold your peace! and it should be your wisdom." He wants the silence back.

At the very end of the book, God turns to Eliphaz and says: "My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath."
The careful explainers are told they were wrong; the man who protested, the book says, spoke what is right.

teach.h: AN EXPLANATION CAN PROTECT THE EXPLAINER.

teach.b: Some readers notice that the friends' theory protects the friends. If suffering always has a reason, then good behavior is a kind of safety, and what happened to Job can't happen to them.
That might be why explanations come so fast, at bedsides and in kitchens. The book's first chapter and its last both refuse their reason.

how: Jews and Christians read the speeches of Job's friends in different ways; some readers take them, and God's words in Job 42:7, as a warning against explaining another person's pain.

games.why: Eliphaz asks who ever perished, being innocent, and the friends build a long case from it; at the end, God says they were wrong.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose trouble you know about, a diagnosis, a breakup, a lost job, and watch whether your mind offers an explanation: well, they never listened. If one comes, notice it, and notice whom it comforts.
Then set it down unspoken and come back to the person and how heavy their day must be, staying with them instead of the reason.
